chapter_title: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
learning_objective: The learner will attribute each of eight teacher comments to the innovation attribute that is the barrier, correctly attributing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** which-attribute-is-the-barrier
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** attribute
**Learning Objective:** The learner will attribute each of eight teacher comments to the innovation attribute that is the barrier, correctly attributing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability (all defined in the section "The Five Innovation Attributes" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 8 teacher comments in one of five attribute bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Barrier attribute" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the attribute definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Every adoption problem is a training problem. (2) Teachers who do not adopt are resistant. (3) Complexity and compatibility are the same. **Instructional Rationale:** Attributing a comment to an attribute requires reading the reason behind it, such as a fit problem, a difficulty problem, or a visibility problem. Comments that sound alike but differ in cause, such as "doesn't fit my schedule" and "too hard to use," make the learner separate the attributes. **Content:** Five attributes with definitions on request: | Attribute | Definition shown | |---|---| | Relative advantage | Perceived as better than what it replaces | | Compatibility | Consistent with existing values, practices, and needs | | Complexity | Perceived as difficult to understand and use | | Trialability | Can be tried on a limited basis | | Observability | Results are visible to others | Eight comments: | # | Teacher comment shown to the learner | Barrier attribute | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | "It doesn't match the weekly pacing guide I am required to follow." | Compatibility | It conflicts with an existing requirement. | | 2 | "I spent an hour and still couldn't get the students logged in." | Complexity | The tool is perceived as hard to use. | | 3 | "I don't see why this is any better than the workbook I already use." | Relative advantage | The benefit over the current practice is not clear. | | 4 | "I'd try it for a unit, but the contract is for three years with no exit." | Trialability | It cannot be tried on a limited basis. | | 5 | "I've never seen a class using it, so I can't picture how it would go." | Observability | The results are not visible to the teacher. | | 6 | "It would mean giving up the group discussions that I believe in." | Compatibility | It conflicts with a practice the teacher values. | | 7 | "The sign-in, the settings, and the dashboard are too much to learn." | Complexity | It is perceived as too complicated. | | 8 | "Nobody in our school can tell me what difference it made." | Observability | The benefit is not visible to others. | **Provenance:** Definitions follow the chapter section "The Five Innovation Attributes" and Rogers (2003). The comments are illustrative, written for this chapter. **Rules:** Each comment has exactly one barrier attribute, given in Content. A comment is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one comment at a time and the five attributes. 2. The learner places the comment and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct attribute and reason are shown. 4. After all 8 comments, the sim shows the score and the misplaced comments with their correct attributes. 5. The learner should notice that two comments each point to compatibility, complexity, and observability, and that none of them is a matter of willingness. **Feedback:** 8 comments, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [attribute]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the attribute]." After the second attempt the correct attribute is revealed and the comment counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can name the barrier behind a comment." For a score < 7: "Review the five attributes and try again; the comments will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Comment 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five attributes, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which attribute is the barrier?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists five attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability) and the Eastside barrier diagnosis. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.
